T1.text:
**Table Report for Plenary:**

As a student who has dropped out before, I found Q3.4 on Absalon data particularly challenging because it raises significant privacy concerns. While some may see moderate improvements as acceptable, my preference is for "never" due to the invasive nature of tracking online activity.

For me, the most important questions were Q6.1 on intervention preferences and Q7.2 on personalized messages. These questions highlight the need for flexible support that respects student agency and privacy.

Our table discussed how answers differed on Q3.4 and Q3.5 on disability-related information. While some saw moderate improvements as sufficient, others—like me—believed larger gains were necessary to justify using sensitive data. Ultimately, our discussion reinforced the importance of balancing accuracy with privacy while prioritizing student-centered outreach methods.

We also came up with a new idea: maybe students could opt into certain types of data collection or intervention preferences, giving them more control over how they are supported. This way, the system would feel less intrusive and more respectful of individual needs.

As a student advisor who has worked closely with students experiencing academic difficulties, I found Q3.4 on Absalon data particularly tough because it feels intrusive and could make students uncomfortable. While I initially leaned toward "never," hearing others' perspectives made me consider that moderate improvements might be acceptable if they significantly help identify at-risk students.

The most important questions for me were Q6.1 on intervention preferences and Q7.2 about personalized messages. Flexibility in outreach methods is key to ensuring support feels respectful rather than intrusive.

Our table discussed differences in opinions on sensitive data, particularly disability-related information (Q3.5). While some saw small improvements as sufficient, I believed moderate gains were necessary to justify using such data—especially considering the ethical implications.

We also explored an idea not covered in the survey: involving students directly in shaping the predictive model by allowing them to contribute anonymized insights on what types of support have worked best for them. This collaborative approach could enhance both trust and effectiveness in the system.

T2.text:
Our table found Q4.1 and Q6.1 the most important for model design: transparency builds trust, especially for students who might hesitate to seek help, while the type of intervention shapes willingness to engage with support.

Some answers differed on moderate explainability—some said "small" improvement was acceptable, others "never". This reflects differing views on balancing accuracy and clarity. For interventions, most preferred generic emails or meeting invitations over personalized messages due to privacy concerns, and twice-yearly outreach struck the best balance between proactive support and respecting boundaries.

One idea outside the survey is ensuring students have a way to opt out of contact if they find it overwhelming—a key consideration for mental well-being.

Thank you, S4, for that thorough overview. As a student advisor, I'd like to add that while explainability and intervention types are crucial, we should also consider how selectivity balances effectiveness with respect for students' privacy.

The differing views on moderate explainability highlight the tension between transparency and reaching more students in need. For interventions, ensuring personalized outreach is handled sensitively can make a significant difference in student engagement without feeling invasive.

Additionally, we discussed the importance of continuous feedback loops—where students can share their experiences with the system—to refine how support is offered over time, fostering trust and improving outcomes. This adaptive approach ensures that the model evolves alongside the needs of the diverse student population it serves.

T3.text:
As a student with dyslexia, I found Q5.1 particularly challenging—accepting any accuracy loss feels tough when support is at stake. Our table agrees that equalizing recall across groups (Q5.2) and balancing outreach methods (Q6/Q7) are crucial.

We discussed why some accepted higher accuracy losses for fairness—they likely see firsthand how inequalities impact students, making this trade-off necessary despite small risks of missing someone in need.

One idea we didn’t capture in the survey is involving student representatives in designing the model. They could ensure it addresses real challenges while respecting privacy concerns.

As an advisor, I found Q5.1 challenging because even small decreases in identifying students experiencing academic difficulties can have significant impacts on their academic success and well-being. Our table agrees that ensuring equal recall across student groups (Q5.2) is essential.

We discussed why some participants accepted higher accuracy losses for fairness—it likely reflects a deeper understanding of how systemic inequalities disproportionately affect certain student groups, making this trade-off necessary despite the risks.

One additional idea our table had was to provide clear communication about the purpose and limitations of the model. Transparency could help build trust and ensure that students understand the support being offered without feeling overly monitored or stigmatized.
